newsitem.title: peru: Little headway reported in Peru hostage talks.
newsitem.headline: Little headway reported in Peru hostage talks.

text.p: There was no visible progress in talks to end Peru's hostage siege on Friday, but there were signs of growing strain among the 72 captives after 12 weeks under the gun.

Mediators met on Thursday with rebel leader Nestor Cerpa, a guerrilla veteran, to explore ways of ending the standoff at the Japanese ambassador's home where the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels are holding the hostages.
But the mediators, members of a three-man guarantors commission, gave no sign of any progress in the talks and did not say when the next round of talks might be held.
The constant to-and-fro of meetings between the mediators and the rebels this week suggested talks were not at a complete deadlock, but nor was anybody reporting any tangible results.

Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, a member of the guarantors' commission, hinted that both sides must relax their positions for progress to be made, saying this week that they needed "a stage of reflection" for talks to move forward.

There were reports of emotional breakdown by one of the captives, Bolivian ambassador Jose Gumucio, who apparently quarreled angrily with a rebel who threatened him with a gun, according to a police source. Other hostages intervened to calm the ambassador, the source said.
In La Paz, a Bolivian government minister said the argument began when Gumucio objected to "offensive" statements about Bolivia made by one of the hostage-takers.

Gumucio reacted "in a brave and serene way in the face of this provocation, and was answered in an improper way by one of the kidnappers. It all concluded with the intervention of other people present," Bolivia's social communication minister, Mauricio Balcazar, told reporters.

The episode -- the most serious of its kind known to have happened during the siege -- suggested tension between the rebels and the hostages was rising. Lima televison reports said Gumucio suffered an attack of hysteria.

A doctor accompanying Red Cross medical teams said this week that many of the hostages and a few of the rebels were suffering stress-related disorders, like inflamed gums, skin ailments and hair loss.

President Alberto Fujimori, trying to show the affairs of government carrying on normally despite the crisis, continued travelling around the country with a visit on Thursday night to the northern department of Cajamarca.
The president spent much of the week in former strongholds of the MRTA in the remote San Martin department, railing against the rebel group and insisting it was bereft of popular support.

Three months after about 20 heavily armed rebels stormed a cocktail party at the ambassador's home and took hundreds of guests captive, the two sides appear no closer to resolving the main rebel demand -- freedom for jailed comrades.

Fujimori has said he would never consider releasing them from jail but would be flexible on other points, even travelling to Cuba last month to arrange asylum for the hostage-takers as an incentive to free the captives.

In a sign of progress on asylum, the Japanese government announced that a top foreign ministry official would be travelling to Cuba and the Dominican Republic next week to seek their cooperation in case the hostage-takers accept exile in those countries.
Vice foreign minister Masahiko Komura will leave Tokyo on Monday for a one-week visit to Peru and later the two Caribbean nations, chief government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama said.
"There is a valid reason for visiting those nations after visiting Peru, and one can say such coordination will take place," Kajiyama said in Tokyo.
"It is time for making such preparations. Progress is underway," Kajiyama said.
Attention has turned to the possibility that the government might resort to force to free the hostages.

"The government is looking for a negotiated solution but if dialogue does not lead anywhere, it cannot stand there with its arms folded. The possibility of using force becomes stronger," said police general Hector Jhon Caro, a former chief of the anti-terrorism police.
